questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Courses and country

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I give it not 10, because I had a not so good studying experience at my faculty. But the social and cultural experience made it all worth it. I will also write a disclaimer here, saying that most of my critiques below concerns the Faculty of Mathematics, Information and Mechanics, and other Erasmus students I got to know from other faculties had a better experience.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: General information about the university was fairly easy to find, but there was given absolutely no information about or introduction to specifically my study or faculty. This was pretty bad, I had to find out everything myself through websites and teachers and other students. I strongly recommend asking the international coordinator related to your faculty for help and guidance.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I was offered a mentor (a student from the university to help settle in the city), which I declined, but in hindsight it would have been helpful to have someone tell relevant information about the faculty.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Again, I got no information or orientation specifically about my study, you really have to write and ask coordinators yourself about everything. But this is maybe different for the bigger larger faculties, I think they got more information and an introduction.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
If you have a low budget, there are options for renting a room in shared flat through Erasmus housing portals such as Pepehousing.
I prioritised privacy and location, so I found an apartment on my own via
rentflatpoland.com
. It was difficult to find an apartment in the area I wanted, Srodmiescie Poludniowe, which I think is the most lively local area with many cafes, restaurants, shops etc. But there were a fair share of options outside of this district, for less than 4000 kr.
I tried to find an apartment on polish apartment portals, but I got rejected or not answered, since I did not speak polish and/or only wanted to rent for half a year. I wasted a lot of time on this, so I would recommend not to bother and just use the websites made for foreigners/international students.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I think it was great to live in an area surrounded by locals and not only among other students, and to try to build a base and home in another country. But it is all about what you prefer and your budget of course.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The university only offered shared rooms in dorms, no options for renting a single room. But they were cheap!

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The process of choosing courses and registering was a bit chaotic for me, but I think I also made it hard for myself by trying to figure everything out by myself.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It depends on the courses you wish to take. The course registration periods are different for different faculties. When it comes to registration, some courses you can register yourself on USOSweb, which is the student platform like KUnet. Other courses the faculty coordinator has to register for you.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You could write the faculty coordinators for help on e-mail.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got registered for all the courses I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
I lost a lot of time trying to figure out registration to courses at different faculties on my own. It is very confusing and there was different information on different sites. Just find the courses that you wish to take, and then write the faculty coordinators and ask how to register. My faculty coordinator was very helpful in registering and un-registering me to courses. I also found that the registration period was different for Erasmus students than regular students. I think it is also a good idea to ask for a meeting with the faculty coordinator just to find out how everything works on this particular faculty. 

USOSweb has a course catalogue, use this for finding courses. Also write to the course coordinator or professor associated to each course about prerequisites, level, course participation and examination method even though there are some information on USOSweb. I experienced that the courses I took had prerequisites not stated on the course page, so I had to cancel them, find new courses and restructure my whole schedule, which was tedious. So find som backup courses! 
Furthermore, the professors were very flexible in regards to examination method, which was both good and bad. Examination dates were rescheduled, suddenly I had to do assignments not stated on the course page, and an oral part of the examination was also possible even though on USOSweb it said only written. So talk to them before the course and talk about expectations to the course.
This can of course be different on different faculties and studies!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I actually think that the university has some interesting courses, I just was not ready for the academic level. But they have some cool year-long seminar courses with focus on research, which I would have taken if I was on exchange for a year or in the beginning of the academic year.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The academic level for me seemed high, and I think this is because the teaching style was very different in the courses I took at UW, than what I am used to on MATH at UCPH. The teaching style together with the smaller classes results in a more loose and intuition-based teaching rather than  technical and thorough as I experience it at UCPH.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: There was not may people attending the courses that I chose, and it was my impression that there was not as many people enrolled in Mathematics as at UCPH. The smaller classes together with the fact that often course participation counts into the examination assessment, means that the teaching is often very discussion-based. At UCPH I am used to separate lectures by the professor and then exercise sessions with a TA, but at UW the two things sometimes was mixed together and the professor conducted all of the 2x90 minutes of teaching each week. The structure of the courses was often very loose. In most of my classes no curriculum was stated and almost no information given about classes on an online platform. Everything happened at the classes, so ask the professor if you want to know curriculum for next class beforehand.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
I took the following math courses: Differential Geometry, Algebraic Topology and Number Theory.
I then also took two courses outside of math: Geography of the World, and Educational Walking Tours in Warsaw.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend Number Theory, as the teacher is very good and the theory is nice. I would also recommend Educational Walking Tours in Warsaw, it is a fun way to get to know the city and meet other international students!

questions.answer: Nothing I remember.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: In general, Warsaw is much cheaper than in Copenhagen, and a nice coffee is only about 20 kr. But watch out, because everything is so cheap you want to go out all the time, and adapt a new lifestyle, and probably you end up spending more money than you would in Copenhagen.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Due to Covid there was only one physical event in the introduction week - a campus tour only of the main campus. 
Else there was Erasmus parties and events, but they were not for me - I think I was a bit too old for the particular clubs.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There was language exchanging events, city game events, trips to other cities, sports tournament weekend in the south of Poland, and Erasmus parties at some clubs.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend the city trips and language exchanging events, they were chill ways to get to know other people.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
I really enjoyed the techno clubs and jazz clubs. In general the area Srodmiescie Poludniowe is super nice. 
I recommend cafes at Plac Zbawiciela; going to free Chopin concerts on Sundays in the summer at the Chopin monument in Lazienki park; use the university library BUW and its garden; drinking at night by the Vistula river (the only place it is allowed to drink in public); go to Bazar na Kole in the weekend; the museum of modern art Zacheta; the Jewish cemetery; try milk bars (cheap good polish food); and in general explore by bike all the weird, different districts.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: The polish seem very closed and not very accommodating. I found it difficult arriving in winter and the city seeming dead and cold and people unhappy. For example strangers often think you are weird if you smile to them in supermarkets, and the service at restaurants/cafes are often not super kind and bad. But this is just how it is, and a reason for this is also that people can get uncomfortable by speaking english. But you get used to it quickly, and as soon as the summer arrived and the weather got better, the city totally blossomed and there are many green areas and people seem happier!

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Just talk to them even if they seem reserved and not interested. My experience was that they would not say hello or start an interaction, but as soon as I took initiative they actually wanted to talk.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: That the polish people are very closed and reserved people.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The food! And the city is actually very international. I also appreciated that they valued being quiet and behave properly, and I also felt very safe in the city (probably due to the fact that it is forbidden to drink in public).

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Be prepared for very unstructured and/or flexible teaching, and consider the benefits of this. 
Ask for help - do not try to figure things out by yourself.
Warsaw is so great and interesting, it seems at first like a strange disrupted place, but use time on understanding the history of the city and talking to local people. You will learn to love the contrasts in the city and the culture!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: My main advice: Unless you want to go on exchange exclusively for studying, you will regret having to use a lot on time on studying, if you also interested in actually getting to know the city and making friends. So choose courses you think you can overcome easily, while also using a lot on time on socialising!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting some like-minded people from other countries, that I consider friends for life, and experiencing a country with such a different history than Denmark.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Trying to figure out a balance between studying and having a life outside the university.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Warsaw is really an interesting city, and worth getting to know! I really fell in love with it. I think I would have a very different, perhaps worse experience if I went there on winter semester. Go for summer semester!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
